mainTopic: The forgiveness of שאול, the spelling of מאברין/מעברין, and stories of precise, clever and careless speech
overview: This amud finishes the side discussion about שאול. רבי יוחנן proves from a verse that he was forgiven for the sin of נוב. The גמרא then returns to the spelling question of מאברין or מעברין. בני יהודה, known for precise speech, answer that both versions are taught. The גמרא contrasts the exact speech of בני יהודה with the sloppy, comical speech of בני גליל. It then brings examples of clever coded speech (לשון חכמה) from רבי's maidservant, רבי יוסי בר אסיין, רבי אבהו and רבי אלעאי. Next, רבי יהושע בן חנניה tells how a woman, a young girl and a young boy each beat him in words. The amud ends with stories of ברוריה's sharp wisdom: she corrects רבי יוסי הגלילי for using too many words, then comes across a student learning in a whisper. Her reaction to the student comes on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the verse about שאול
steps.stepSummary: This amud opens with the last word of a verse about שאול, ending the proof that came on the previous amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: "...he would do them harm."
steps.whatsHappening: This is just the final word of a verse that the גמרא was already quoting about שאול. It closes off the previous point before the גמרא moves on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse (שמואל א יד:מז) was brought as a source about שאול. It was part of a contrast between שאול and דוד. Because the verse sounds critical of שאול, the very next step adds a softening, positive note about him.

keyTerms.meaning: He would do harm / act against them (the closing word of the verse)

phrases.english: "...he would do them harm."
phrases.notes: The tail end of a verse (שמואל א יד:מז) whose quotation began on the previous amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a verse that began earlier.
steps.raayaObject: The earlier point about שאול, which contrasted him with דוד.

steps.title: שאול was forgiven for the sin of נוב
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן proves from a verse that הקדוש ברוך הוא forgave שאול for his sin. The proof is that שמואל told him, "tomorrow you and your sons will be with me," meaning in שמואל's place in heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: How do we know that הקדוש ברוך הוא forgave שאול for that sin (killing the כהנים of נוב)? Because the verse says, "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me." "With me" means in my section, alongside me.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן ends the talk about שאול on a positive note. He shows from a verse that שאול was forgiven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sin meant here is the killing of the כהנים of נוב. The proof rests on one word, "עמי" (with me). שמואל was a צדיק, so being placed "with him" means being on his level in עולם הבא. That could only happen if the sin had been forgiven.

keyTerms.meaning: In my partition, meaning my place or level in heaven

steps.whatToRemember: שאול was forgiven. The word "עמי" teaches that he joined שמואל's level after his death.
steps.confusionAlert: "With me" does not just mean "you will also die." The גמרא reads it as "in my מחיצה," meaning the same spiritual level as שמואל.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִין שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, forgave him
for that sin?
phrases.notes: The killing of the כהנים of נוב.

phrases.english: As it says: "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me."
phrases.notes: שמואל's words to שאול (שמואל א כח:יט).

phrases.english: "With me" means in my partition (on my level).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מִנַּיִין שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Balances the critical verse about שאול with a statement that he was forgiven.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקדוש ברוך הוא forgave שאול for the sin of נוב, as shown by the word "עמי."

steps.title: רבי אבא wants to ask בני יהודה about the spelling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the spelling question. רבי אבא says that בני יהודה, who are careful with words, would know whether the משנה says מאברין or מעברין, and whether it says אכוזו or עכוזו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said: If someone could ask the people of Judea, who are precise in their language, whether we learned "מאברין" or "מעברין," and whether we learned "אכוזו" or "עכוזו," they would know.
steps.whatsHappening: The side discussion is over, and the גמרא goes back to its earlier question about how to spell a word in the משנה. רבי אבא is setting up the next step: someone should go and ask בני יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מאברין (with א) suggests adding a "limb" (אבר) to the city. מעברין (with ע) suggests making it "pregnant" (עוברה), like a filled-out shape. רבי אבא adds a second spelling question of the same type, אכוזו or עכוזו, a term in a משנה about a firstborn animal's hindquarters. Earlier the גמרא praised בני יהודה for their precise language, so they are the natural people to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: Who are precise in their language
Extending a city's boundary, spelled with א or with ע
Its hindquarters, spelled with א or with ע

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אִיכָּא דִּמְשַׁאֵיל לְהוּ לִבְנֵי יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: If there is someone who would ask the people of Judea
who are precise in their language
did we learn "me'abrin" (with alef) or "me'abrin" (with ayin)?
Did we learn "akuzo" (with alef) or "akuzo" (with ayin)?
phrases.notes: A term for an animal's hindquarters.

phrases.english: They would know.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא: אִי אִיכָּא דִּמְשַׁאֵיל לְהוּ לִבְנֵי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story about שאול and returns to the earlier spelling question about the word in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the correct reading מאברין or מעברין, and is it אכוזו or עכוזו?

steps.title: Both spellings are taught
steps.stepSummary: They asked בני יהודה, who answered that both versions exist: some teach מאברין and some teach מעברין, and likewise some teach אכוזו and some teach עכוזו.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked them, and they answered: Some teach "מאברין" and some teach "מעברין." Some teach "אכוזו" and some teach "עכוזו."
steps.whatsHappening: Someone actually asks בני יהודה. They answer that both spellings are accepted and taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rather than picking one correct version, the answer confirms that both readings have a real basis. Each spelling carries its own meaning: "adding a limb" or "making it pregnant." Neither version is a mistake.
steps.whatToRemember: Both מאברין and מעברין are valid readings, and so are אכוזו and עכוזו. Each spelling hints at a different picture of the same law.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer is not "we don't know." It is a positive answer: both traditions are correct.

phrases.english: They asked them, and they said to him:
Some teach "me'abrin" (with alef),
and some teach "me'abrin" (with ayin).
Some teach "akuzo" (with alef),
and some teach "akuzo" (with ayin).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers רבי אבא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both versions are taught: מאברין and מעברין, and אכוזו and עכוזו.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both spellings are legitimate traditions, so neither reading is an error.

steps.title: What does it mean that בני יהודה are precise in speech?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for an example of how בני יהודה are careful with language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of יהודה are careful with language. What does that mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up the phrase 'בני יהודה דייקי לישנא' from the earlier discussion and asks what it looks like in real life. This sets up the story that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, רבי אבא sent the question to בני יהודה because they are careful with words. Now the גמרא stops to explain that description. It wants a concrete case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? (What does this mean?)

phrases.english: The people of Judea are precise in language
what is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה דָּיְיקִי לִישָּׁנָא מַאי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Side question about the description of בני יהודה used in step 3
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of the precise speech of בני יהודה

steps.title: The man from יהודה selling a cloak 'like beets on the ground'
steps.stepSummary: A man from יהודה described the color of his cloak with a very exact picture: the green of young beet leaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man from יהודה said: 'I have a cloak to sell.' People asked him: 'What color is your cloak?' He answered: 'Like beets on the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a story. A man from יהודה gave a very exact description of a color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did not just say 'green.' He named the exact shade, the color of beet leaves when they first come up from the earth. This shows how carefully בני יהודה choose their words.

phrases.english: As in the case of a certain man from Judea
who said to them:
I have a cloak to sell.
They said to him: What color is your cloak?
He said to them: Like beets on the ground.
phrases.notes: The exact green of young beet leaves sprouting from the earth

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A Judean described his cloak's color with exact precision: 'like beets on the ground.'

steps.title: What does it mean that בני גליל are not precise?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks for an example of the opposite: how בני גליל are not careful with language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The people of גליל are not careful with language. What does that mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the contrast and asks what the careless speech of בני גליל looks like. This sets up the stories that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The precision of יהודה is easier to understand next to the carelessness of גליל. The גמרא now asks for examples of that weakness.

phrases.english: The people of the Galilee, who are not precise in language
what is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי גָלִיל דְּלָא דָּיְיקִי לִישָּׁנָא מַאי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel question about the opposite group
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of the imprecise speech of בני גליל

steps.title: The man from גליל shouting 'Who wants amar?'
steps.stepSummary: A man from גליל called out 'אמר' but did not pronounce his guttural letters clearly. Nobody could tell which of four different words he meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: a man from גליל walked around saying, 'Who wants amar? Who wants amar?' People told him: 'Foolish Galilean! Do you mean a donkey to ride, wine to drink, wool to wear, or a lamb to slaughter?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a story showing how unclear Galilean speech was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words חמור/חמר (with ח), עמר (with ע) and אימר (with א) sound different only if you pronounce the guttural letters properly. The Galilean blurred them all, so his word could mean four completely different things. This ties back to the earlier question of מאברין versus מעברין, where the difference is also an א versus an ע.
steps.confusionAlert: The same sound 'חמר' could mean both donkey and wine. That is why there are four options here, not three.

phrases.english: As it was taught: that a certain man from the Galilee
was walking around and saying to people:
"Amar for whom? Amar for whom?"
phrases.notes: He slurred the first letter, a throaty sound, so it came out unclear.

phrases.english: They said to him: Foolish Galilean,
a donkey to ride, or wine to drink?
wool to wear, or a lamb to slaughter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A Galilean's unclear guttural letters made 'amar' mean four different things.

steps.title: The woman who meant to offer milk but said 'may a lioness eat you'
steps.stepSummary: A Galilean woman meant to invite her friend to eat milk. Because she slurred her words, it came out as a curse: 'may a lioness eat you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman wanted to say to her friend: 'Come, let me feed you milk.' Instead she said: 'My neighbor, may a lioness eat you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another example of Galilean careless speech, this time with a funny result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'דאוכליך חלבא' (I will feed you milk) slurred into 'תוכליך לביא' (a lioness will eat you). Swallowing letters and blurring sounds turned a kind offer into a curse. This adds force to the claim that בני גליל were not precise.

phrases.english: A certain woman who wanted
to say to her friend:
"Come, and I will feed you milk,"
instead said to her:
"My neighbor, may a lioness eat you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example supporting the same point as step 8
steps.raayaObject: The claim that בני גליל are not precise in speech
steps.raayaSupportSource: Story of the woman whose invitation became a curse

steps.title: The woman before the judge who accidentally insulted him
steps.stepSummary: A Galilean woman came to complain to a judge that her board was stolen. Her slurred words came out as calling him a servant, saying he was stolen, and describing a beam he could be hanged on.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman came before a judge and said: 'My master, servant, I had a beam and they stole you from me. It was so big that if they hung you on it, your feet would not reach the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a final example. Unclear speech turned a court complaint into an insult to the judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She meant 'מרי קירי' (my master, sir), but it sounded like 'כירי' (servant). She meant 'they stole it from me' (וגנבוה מיני), but it came out as 'they stole you' (וגנבוך מין). Her description of the large beam then sounded like a threat to hang the judge, showing how far careless speech can go.

keyTerms.meaning: Meant 'my master, sir', but came out as 'master, servant'

steps.whatToRemember: בני יהודה were exact speakers (the cloak 'like beets on the ground'). בני גליל blurred their sounds, which caused confusion and accidental insults. That is why the spelling question (א or ע) was sent to בני יהודה.

phrases.english: A certain woman who came before a judge
said to him: "My master, servant,"
phrases.notes: She meant קירי (sir) but said כירי (servant)

phrases.english: I had a beam
and they stole you from me.
phrases.notes: She meant 'they stole it from me'

phrases.english: And it was so large
that when they would hang you on it,
your feet would not reach the ground."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third example supporting the same point
steps.raayaObject: The claim that בני גליל are not precise in speech
steps.raayaSupportSource: Story of the woman whose complaint to a judge became an insult

steps.title: רבי's maidservant signals that the wine is finished
steps.stepSummary: The maidservant in רבי's house used a poetic riddle to tell the students that the wine was gone and it was time to go home.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the maidservant of רבי's household spoke in coded, wise language, she would say: 'The ladle is knocking against the jug. Let the eagles fly to their nests.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now switches from the bad examples of בני גליל to good examples of clever, refined speech, starting with רבי's maidservant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her riddle had two parts. 'The ladle knocks against the jug' means the ladle is hitting the bottom, so the wine jug is almost empty. 'Let the eagles fly to their nests' means the students (the 'eagles') should go home, all said politely and without embarrassing anyone.

keyTerms.meaning: Wise or coded language, speaking in riddles
Ladle used to draw wine from a jug
Eagles, a code word here for the students

steps.confusionAlert: Even though this is a woman speaking, she is NOT another bad example like the Galilean women. She is the opposite: an example of beautiful, careful speech from רבי's house.

phrases.english: The maidservant of the house of Rabbi
when she would speak in wise (coded) language,
phrases.notes: Speaking in riddles or euphemisms

phrases.english: she would say like this:
The ladle is knocking against the jug,
phrases.notes: The wine is nearly finished

phrases.english: let the eagles fly to their nests.
phrases.notes: The students should go home

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמְהֲתָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי כִּי הֲוָה מִשְׁתַּעְיָא בִּלְשׁוֹן חׇכְמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with the sloppy Galilean speech in steps 8-10 by showing refined, careful speech.
steps.raayaObject: The refined, careful speech that the גמרא praises, the opposite of בני גליל
steps.raayaSupportSource: The coded speech of רבי's maidservant

steps.title: רבי's maidservant signals that the students should stay
steps.stepSummary: When רבי wanted the students to stay, the maidservant used another riddle to announce that a fresh jug of wine was being opened.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he wanted them to sit, she would say to them: 'Let the stopper be removed from the next jug, and let the ladle float in the jug like a ship sailing in the sea.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the same story and gives the maidservant's opposite message: stay, there is more wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Opening the 'friend' jug means opening a new, full jug. A ladle floating like a ship pictures a jug filled to the top, so the students know they are welcome to stay.

keyTerms.meaning: Its friend, meaning the next jug

phrases.english: And when he wanted them to sit (stay),
she would say to them:
Let [the stopper] be removed from the jug next to it,
phrases.notes: Open a new jug

phrases.english: and let the ladle float in the jug,
like a ship sailing in the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite message from the same maidservant (stay instead of leave).
steps.raayaObject: The refined, careful speech of רבי's household

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר אסיין asks for beets in mustard in code
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר אסיין built a coded request out of translated words. 'An ox in judgment on a poor mountain' secretly meant beets in mustard.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוסי בר אסיין spoke in coded language, he said: 'Make for me an ox in judgment on a poor mountain.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second example of clever speech, this time from a sage who made word puzzles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word is translated into the other language and the pieces are joined. Ox = תור and judgment = דין, which together sound like תרדין (beets). Mountain = הר (said 'חר') and poor = דל, which together make חרדל (mustard). So he was asking for beets in mustard.

keyTerms.meaning: Beets in mustard, the hidden meaning

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Asyan,
when he would speak in wise (coded) language,
he said: Make for me an ox in judgment
phrases.notes: תור + דין = תרדין, beets

phrases.english: on a poor mountain.
phrases.notes: חר + דל = חרדל, mustard

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר אָסְיָין כִּי הֲוָה מִשְׁתַּעֵי בִּלְשׁוֹן חׇכְמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second person who used clever, coded speech.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוסי בר אסיין's word puzzle for beets in mustard

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר אסיין asks about the innkeeper in code
steps.stepSummary: When asking about an inn, רבי יוסי בר אסיין built the word for innkeeper out of translated syllables and asked what good food was available.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he asked about an inn, he said: 'Man, here, this, raw: what good is there?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more word puzzle from רבי יוסי בר אסיין. The series of clever-speech examples continues in the next steps with רבי אבהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word is translated to Hebrew: man = איש, here (mouth) = פה, this = זה, raw = נא. Together they sound like 'אושפיזכנא', innkeeper. So he was asking the innkeeper what good things he had to offer.
steps.whatToRemember: Steps 8-10 showed בני גליל whose careless speech caused confusion and insults. Steps 11-14 show the opposite: people who used language so precisely that they could hide whole messages in it.

phrases.english: And when he would ask about an inn,
he would say like this:
Man, here, this, raw,
phrases.notes: איש + פה + זה + נא = innkeeper

phrases.english: what good is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second coded phrase from the same sage.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוסי בר אסיין's coded question about the innkeeper

steps.title: רבי אבהו orders roosters in code
steps.stepSummary: When רבי אבהו spoke in clever language, he asked for the coals to be fanned until they glowed and for two roosters to be roasted. He described these things only through riddles.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי אבהו spoke cleverly, he would say: 'Make the coals the color of an אתרוג, spread out the golden ones, and make me two speakers-in-the-dark.' Some say the version was: 'And let them make me on them two speakers-in-the-dark.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more example of a Sage speaking in coded, clever language. רבי אבהו asks for a roasted-chicken meal without ever plainly saying 'coals' or 'roosters.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each phrase hides a simple object. 'Make the coals like an אתרוג' means fan them until they glow yellow-orange, 'spread the golden ones' means spread out the glowing coals, and 'speakers-in-the-dark' means roosters, which crow before dawn. The second version (איכא דאמרי) adds 'on them' to make it clear the roosters should be roasted on those coals.

keyTerms.meaning: Make like an אתרוג (make glow yellow-orange)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Speakers-in-the-dark' are not people. They are roosters, which 'announce' the morning while it is still dark.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu, when he would speak
in clever language, would say like this:
Make the coals like an etrog,
phrases.notes: Fan them until they glow yellow-orange.

phrases.english: spread out the golden ones,
phrases.notes: The glowing coals look like gold.

phrases.english: and make me two speakers-in-the-dark.
phrases.notes: Two roosters.

phrases.english: Some say:

phrases.aramaic: וְיַעֲשׂוּ לִי בָּהֶן שְׁנֵי מַגִּידֵי בַּעֲלָטָה.
phrases.english: And let them make me on them two speakers-in-the-dark.
phrases.notes: Roast the roosters on those coals.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ כִּי הֲוָה מִשְׁתַּעֵי בִּלְשׁוֹן חׇכְמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another example in the series of coded speech, like רבי יוסי בר אסיין's food requests.
steps.raayaObject: That the Sages were skilled in clever, coded speech
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבהו's riddle ordering roasted roosters

steps.title: The Rabbis ask where רבי אלעאי is hiding
steps.stepSummary: The Rabbis ask רבי אבהו, using a word-play on 'hidden,' where רבי אלעאי is. This sets up his riddle answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis said to רבי אבהו: 'Reveal to us where רבי אלעאי is hidden.'
steps.whatsHappening: The Rabbis ask רבי אבהו a question in clever language. This step is setting up his coded answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They use two words from the same root, צפן (hidden): 'הצפינונו' and 'צפון.' The play on words shows they are joining in the clever-speech style. They want to know why רבי אלעאי has not shown up.

keyTerms.meaning: Show us / reveal to us (word-play on 'hidden')

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rabbi Abbahu:
Show us where Rabbi Elai is hidden.
phrases.notes: Both key words come from the root צפן (hide).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about רבי אבהו and clever speech.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where רבי אלעאי is and why he is absent

steps.title: רבי אבהו answers with a riddle
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers that רבי אלעאי rejoiced with a 'latter Aharonic lively girl' who kept him awake. That is why he is sleeping now.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'He rejoiced with a girl who is Aharonic, the latest one, lively, and she kept him awake.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers the Rabbis' question with a riddle full of sound-alike words. The point is that something kept רבי אלעאי up all night, so he is resting now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He plays on sounds: אהרונית (from אהרן, a כהן family) and אחרונית (the latest one), then עירנית (lively, or from a town) and והנעירתו (kept him awake). The riddle is left open on purpose. The next step explains what the 'girl' could be.

keyTerms.meaning: From the family of אהרן (a כהן family)

phrases.english: He said to them:
He rejoiced with an Aharonic girl,
phrases.notes: From a כהן family, or connected to כהנים.

phrases.english: the latter one, a lively one,
phrases.notes: Sound-play: אהרונית / אחרונית; עירנית / והנעירתו.

phrases.english: and she kept him awake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Rabbis' coded question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעאי was kept awake all night by a 'girl' and is now resting.

steps.title: Two ways to decode the riddle: a wife or a tractate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives two readings of the 'girl': either a new wife, or a new מסכתא that he learned all night.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say it means a woman. And some say it means a tractate.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רבי אבהו's riddle meant, and gives two possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading one: רבי אלעאי married a young second wife from a כהן family, and she kept him up. Reading two: the 'girl' is a מסכתא from סדר קדשים (the 'Aharonic' order about כהנים), his newest learning, which was hard and lively and kept him up studying all night. Either way, he is sleeping now because he was up all night.
steps.whatToRemember: This whole section shows the Sages using clever, coded speech. A riddle can hide simple things like a meal, or a reason someone is missing. רבי אבהו's riddle about רבי אלעאי can mean a new wife or a new מסכתא learned through the night.

phrases.english: Some say it means a woman.
phrases.notes: A young second wife from a כהן family.

phrases.english: And some say it means a tractate.
phrases.notes: A new מסכתא from סדר קדשים, studied all night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decodes the riddle given in step 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'girl' is either a new wife or a new tractate. Either way, רבי אלעאי was up all night and is now resting.

steps.title: The Rabbis ask רבי אלעאי where רבי אבהו is hiding
steps.stepSummary: Now the roles are reversed. The Rabbis use the same 'hidden' word-play to ask רבי אלעאי where רבי אבהו is.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רבי אלעאי: 'Reveal to us where רבי אבהו is hidden.'
steps.whatsHappening: The Rabbis turn to רבי אלעאי and ask, in clever language, where רבי אבהו has gone. This question sets up רבי אלעאי's riddle answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 16, where they asked רבי אבהו about רבי אלעאי. Now רבי אלעאי gets his turn to show clever speech. The word הַצְפִּינֵנוּ plays on צָפוּן ('hidden'), the same word-play used before.

keyTerms.meaning: Reveal to us what is hidden (a play on the root צפן, 'hide')

phrases.english: They said to Rabbi Elai:
Reveal to us where Rabbi Abbahu is hidden.
phrases.notes: Same 'hidden' word-play as in step 16, now aimed the other way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirror image of the question in step 16, after step 18 explained the earlier riddle.

steps.title: רבי אלעאי answers in a riddle: רבי אבהו went south
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעאי says that רבי אבהו consulted 'the one who crowns' and 'went south to מפיבשת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'He took counsel with the one who crowns, and went south to מפיבשת.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעאי answers the question with a riddle. In plain words: רבי אבהו asked permission from the נשיא and went to the Sages of the south.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The one who crowns' (הַמַּכְתִּיר) is the נשיא, who appoints Sages. 'מפיבשת' was the grandson of שאול and a great Sage of his time, so here the name stands for the great Sages of the south. 'הִנְגִּיב' comes from נֶגֶב ('south') and means 'went south.'

keyTerms.meaning: The one who crowns, meaning the נָשִׂיא who appoints Sages
Grandson of King שָׁאוּל and a great Sage; here a code name for the southern Sages

phrases.english: He said to them:
He took counsel with the one who crowns,
phrases.notes: The נשיא, who appoints the Sages.

phrases.english: and went south to Mephibosheth.
phrases.notes: He went to the great Sages of the south.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the riddle question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אבהו got permission from the נשיא and traveled to the Sages of the south.
steps.whatToRemember: The riddle series ends with each Sage answering the other in clever code language. The point of the whole section is to praise sharp, elegant speech.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן חנניה: only a woman, a boy and a girl ever beat me
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן חנניה says that in all his life no one beat him in words except a woman, a young boy and a young girl.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן חנניה said: 'In all my days no person defeated me, except a woman, a young boy and a young girl.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new but related theme: a great Sage who was outsmarted in conversation. This statement sets up three stories, one for each person who beat him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא told about Sages who spoke cleverly. Now it shows that even a giant like רבי יהושע בן חנניה could be beaten by sharp ordinary people. His statement is the heading, and the stories that follow fill it in.

keyTerms.meaning: Defeated me, got the better of me
A young boy and a young girl

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya said:
In all my days, no person defeated me
except a woman, a young boy, and a young girl.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story series on the related theme of clever speech.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only three people ever beat רבי יהושע בן חנניה in words: a woman, a boy and a girl.

steps.title: What happened with the woman?
steps.stepSummary: The text asks what the story with the woman was.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the story of the woman?
steps.whatsHappening: This short question opens the first of the three stories, the one about the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question does not challenge anything. It simply asks for details, and the answer is the story that follows.

phrases.english: What is the story of the woman?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details behind the first item in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the woman got the better of him.

steps.title: The innkeeper's beans: eaten twice, over-salted the third day
steps.stepSummary: At an inn, the hostess served him beans. He finished them completely two days in a row. On the third day she over-salted them, so he stopped eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once I stayed at an inn. She made me beans on the first day; I ate them and left nothing over. On the second day I again left nothing over. On the third day she over-salted them. As soon as I tasted them, I pulled my hands back from them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע begins the story. He finished every bean the first two days. On the third day the beans were too salty, so he stopped eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The detail that he 'left nothing over' matters. Good manners required leaving a little food on the plate. The text does not say why, but it may be that she over-salted the beans on purpose to teach him this. That detail sets up her final jab in step 27.

keyTerms.meaning: She over-salted them, ruined them with salt

phrases.aramaic: פַּעַם אַחַת נִתְאָרַחְתִּי אֵצֶל אַכְסַנְיָא אַחַת,
phrases.english: One time I was a guest at a certain inn,
she made me beans on the first day —
I ate them and left nothing of them over.
The second day, again I left nothing of them over.
On the third day she over-salted them,
as soon as I tasted, I withdrew my hands from them.

steps.triggerLanguage: פַּעַם אַחַת נִתְאָרַחְתִּי אֵצֶל אַכְסַנְיָא אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering 'what happened with the woman.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The setting of the story: two clean plates, then over-salted beans that he left.

steps.title: The hostess asks why he is not eating
steps.stepSummary: The woman asks him why he is not eating the beans.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to me: 'רבי, why are you not eating?'
steps.whatsHappening: The hostess sees him stop eating and asks why. This question sets up his polite excuse in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She knows the reason, because she salted the beans herself. Her question is a test to see how he will explain himself.

phrases.english: She said to me: My Rabbi,
why aren't you eating?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לִי: רַבִּי, מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵינְךָ סוֹעֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to his stopping to eat in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why he stopped eating the beans.

steps.title: His polite excuse: I already ate earlier
steps.stepSummary: Not wanting to embarrass her about the salt, he says he already ate earlier in the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: I said to her: 'I already ate earlier in the day.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives a polite excuse so he will not have to say the food is too salty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His goal is to protect her feelings. But the excuse leaves an opening, and she uses it to catch him in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: While it was still day, earlier in the day

phrases.english: I said to her:
I already ate while it was still day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers her question from step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He claims he is already full from an earlier meal.

steps.title: Her comeback: you should have held back from the bread
steps.stepSummary: She answers that if he ate earlier, he should have eaten less bread at that meal and left room for her beans.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to me: 'You should have pulled your hand back from the bread!'
steps.whatsHappening: The woman turns his excuse against him: if he ate earlier, he should have held back from bread then, to leave room for her beans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His excuse was 'I'm full from an earlier meal.' She answers it: then you should have eaten less bread at that meal and saved room for my beans. This is the first point she scores against him.

keyTerms.meaning: To pull back your hands, to stop eating

phrases.english: She said to me:

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה לְךָ לִמְשׁוֹךְ יָדֶיךָ מִן הַפַּת!
phrases.english: You should have withdrawn your hands from the bread!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לִי: הָיָה לְךָ לִמְשׁוֹךְ יָדֶיךָ מִן הַפַּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the excuse given in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: His claim that he already ate earlier.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he were truly full, he would not be eating bread now. So his excuse is not the real reason.

steps.title: Her teasing guess: maybe you are making up for the first days
steps.stepSummary: She suggests, with a smile, that he is leaving these beans now to make up for not leaving any on the first two days.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to me: 'רבי, perhaps you did not leave a remainder on the first days?'
steps.whatsHappening: The woman jokingly offers her own reason for his leftovers. This sets up the rule of חכמים that she quotes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She hints that he broke etiquette by cleaning his plate twice, and that today's full plate is his 'payback.' Her guess also shows why she salted the beans: to teach him a lesson about manners.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally the corner of a field left for the poor; here, playfully, food left over on the plate
On the first ones, on the earlier days

steps.confusionAlert: פאה here is not the agricultural מצוה of leaving the corner of a field. She borrows the word as a witty name for leftover food on the plate.

phrases.english: She said to me: My Rabbi,
perhaps you did not leave a remainder on the first days?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה לִי: רַבִּי, שֶׁמָּא לֹא הִנַּחְתָּ פֵּאָה בָּרִאשׁוֹנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, sharper jab after step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: His behavior of clearing his plate on the first two days.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Today's leftovers look like a correction for the etiquette he skipped on the earlier days.

steps.title: She backs her jab with a rule of חכמים about leftovers
steps.stepSummary: She quotes חכמים: you do not need to leave food in the pot, but you should leave some on your plate.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Didn't the חכמים say this: One does not leave a remainder in the pot, but one does leave a remainder on the plate.'
steps.whatsHappening: The woman supports her teasing with a rule of manners from חכמים, which ends the story of how she beat him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule separates two places. Food left in the cooking pot (אלפס) is not needed. Food left on one's own plate (קערה) is good manners, so the host sees that the guest was satisfied. By quoting the rule to the great Sage himself, she wins the exchange.
steps.whatToRemember: The woman won by using רבי יהושע's own world, a rule of חכמים, to show that he had broken etiquette by clearing his plate.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story is also a source for the proper manners of leaving a little food on one's plate, which תוספות understands as an expression of etiquette.

phrases.english: And didn't the Sages say this:
One does not leave a remainder in the pot,
but one does leave a remainder on the plate.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the jab of step 27 with a quoted rule.
steps.raayaObject: Her claim that he should have left food on his plate on the earlier days.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A teaching of חכמים: no leftover is needed in the pot, but some should be left on the plate.

steps.title: The young girl questions his walking through a field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the story of the young girl. רבי יהושע בן חנניה tells how he was walking on a path through a field, and a girl asked him, 'Isn't this a field?'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the story of the young girl? One time I was walking on the road. There was a path that went through a field, and I was walking on it. A young girl said to me: 'רבי, isn't this a field?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second person who beat רבי יהושע בן חנניה, the young girl. She challenges him for walking through someone's field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her question is not really a request for information. It is an accusation: walking through a planted field can damage the crops, and that is close to taking what belongs to someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: A field, meaning private land with crops
What is it? Used here to ask for the story behind a reference

phrases.english: What is [the story of] the young girl?
One time I was walking on the road,
and there was a path passing through a field,
and I was walking on it.
A certain young girl said to me:
My teacher, isn't this a field?
phrases.notes: Meaning: you should not be walking here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the story of the woman and the beans, the גמרא moves to the next person on the list.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן חנניה's walking through a field
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A field belongs to its owner, and walking through it may damage the crops.

steps.title: He answers that the path is already well-trodden
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן חנניה defends himself. This is a beaten path that people already walk on, so walking there is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: I said to her: 'No, it is a well-trodden path.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן חנניה answers the girl's challenge. He says the path is already worn down by walkers, so he is not doing any harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A path that has already been trampled is treated as a public way, and there are no crops left on it to ruin. His defense depends on the path already existing.

keyTerms.meaning: A trodden-down path, one that has already been beaten flat by walkers

phrases.aramaic: אָמַרְתִּי לָהּ: לֹא, דֶּרֶךְ כְּבוּשָׁה הִיא.
phrases.english: I said to her: No, it is a well-trodden path.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַרְתִּי לָהּ: לֹא, דֶּרֶךְ כְּבוּשָׁה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the girl's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: this is a public path, not a planted field.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walking here means trampling someone's field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The path is already beaten down, so walking on it is allowed.

steps.title: The girl answers that people like him made the path
steps.stepSummary: The girl rejects his answer. The path only exists because people like him walked through the field when they should not have.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to me: 'Robbers like you trampled it down.'
steps.whatsHappening: The girl knocks down his defense and wins the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His answer assumed the path was a fair, existing road. She points out that the path was created by people wrongly walking through the field. So the path itself came from wrongdoing and cannot excuse him.

keyTerms.meaning: They trod it down, meaning they made it into a path

phrases.english: She said to me:
Robbers like you have trodden it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 30.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that a trodden path makes walking there allowed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The path was made by people trespassing, so it cannot make the trespass permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: The girl won because the 'path' he relied on was itself made by people doing the wrong thing.

steps.title: He asks a boy at a crossroads for directions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the story of the young boy. רבי יהושע בן חנניה met a boy at a fork in the road and asked him which way led to the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the story of the young boy? One time I was walking on the road and I saw a young boy sitting at a crossroads. I said to him: 'Which road should we take to the city?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins the third story, about the young boy. This step sets up the scene and the question that the boy will answer next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבי יהושע בן חנניה simply asks a practical question. The puzzle will come from how the boy answers.

keyTerms.meaning: A crossroads, where the road splits

phrases.english: What is [the story of] the young boy?
One time I was walking on the road,

phrases.aramaic: וְרָאִיתִי תִּינוֹק יוֹשֵׁב עַל פָּרָשַׁת דְּרָכִים.
phrases.english: and I saw a young boy sitting at a crossroads.
And I said to him:
On which road shall we go to the city?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the girl's story to the boy's story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which road leads to the city.

steps.title: The boy describes one road as short and long and the other as long and short
steps.stepSummary: The boy answers with a riddle. One road is 'short and long' and the other is 'long and short.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to me: 'This one is short and long, and that one is long and short.'
steps.whatsHappening: The boy answers the question in a puzzling way. The story will explain what he meant in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'short and long' road is shorter in distance, but it takes longer to actually get into the city. The 'long and short' road is longer in distance, but it gets you there more easily.

keyTerms.meaning: Short and long: short in distance but long in practice
Long and short: long in distance but quicker in practice

phrases.english: He said to me:
This one is short and long,
and that one is long and short.

steps.triggerLanguage: זוֹ קְצָרָה וַאֲרוּכָּה, וְזוֹ אֲרוּכָּה וּקְצָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A riddle-answer that describes each road as both short and long.

steps.title: The short road leads to blocked gardens, so he comes back to complain
steps.stepSummary: He took the short road, but near the city he found gardens and orchards blocking the way. He went back and complained to the boy: 'You told me it was short!'
steps.simpleTranslation: I took the 'short and long' road. When I got near the city, I found gardens and orchards surrounding it. I went back and said to him: 'My son, didn't you tell me it was short?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן חנניה challenges the boy, since the 'short' road did not actually get him into the city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He heard only the word 'short' and acted on it. The gardens and orchards around the city blocked him, so the trip turned out not to be short at all.

phrases.english: And I went on the short-and-long road,
once I reached the city,
I found that gardens and orchards surrounded it.
I turned back.
I said to him: My son,
didn't you tell me it was short?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the boy's directions after following them.
steps.kashyaTarget: The boy's description of the road as 'short'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The road did not actually get him to the city quickly.

steps.title: The boy answers that he also said 'long'
steps.stepSummary: The boy answers that he did warn him. He called that road 'long' too.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to me: 'And didn't I tell you it was long?'
steps.whatsHappening: The boy defends his directions and wins the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The boy had warned him from the start that the short road was also 'long.' רבי יהושע בן חנניה only paid attention to half of the answer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לִי: וְלֹא אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ אֲרוּכָּה?
phrases.english: He said to me: And didn't I tell you it was long?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the complaint in step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points back to the full wording of the original answer.
steps.terutzMaskana: The boy was exact, and the traveler ignored the word 'long'.

steps.title: He kisses the boy and praises the wisdom of all Israel
steps.stepSummary: Impressed, רבי יהושע בן חנניה kisses the boy on the head and praises כלל ישראל: everyone, from old to young, is wise.
steps.simpleTranslation: I kissed him on his head and said to him: 'Fortunate are you, Israel, for all of you are very wise, from your old to your young.'
steps.whatsHappening: The boy's story ends with רבי יהושע בן חנניה admitting defeat and praising the boy's wisdom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of being upset at losing, he turns it into praise of the whole Jewish people. Even a small child has sharp wisdom.

keyTerms.meaning: From your oldest (or greatest) to your youngest

steps.whatToRemember: All three people who beat רבי יהושע בן חנניה (the woman, the girl, the boy) won because they paid close attention to exact words and facts.

phrases.english: I kissed him on his head,
and I said to him:
Fortunate are you, Israel,
for all of you are very wise,
from your old to your young.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁרֵיכֶם יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁכּוּלְּכֶם חֲכָמִים גְּדוֹלִים אַתֶּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the boy's story with praise.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even the youngest Jews have sharp wisdom.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי asks ברוריה for directions to לוד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new story. רבי יוסי הגלילי was traveling, met ברוריה, and asked her which road to take to לוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי הגלילי was walking on the road. He met ברוריה and said to her: 'On which road shall we go to לוד?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a related story about wise speech and a wise woman. This step sets up ברוריה's sharp reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His question has four words: 'באיזו דרך נלך ללוד.' The number of words will be the whole point of her reply.

keyTerms.meaning: ברוריה, the scholarly wife of רבי מאיר

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was walking on the road,
he met Berurya,
he said to her:
On which road shall we go to Lod?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story connected by its theme of wise speech and wise women.

steps.title: ברוריה scolds him for talking too much with a woman
steps.stepSummary: ברוריה calls him a 'foolish Galilean' and reminds him that חכמים said not to talk much with a woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to him: 'Foolish Galilean! Didn't חכמים say: Do not talk too much with a woman?'
steps.whatsHappening: ברוריה challenges the way רבי יוסי הגלילי asked his question. She backs up her point with a teaching of חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She is not objecting to his asking at all. She is objecting to the extra words. She uses the teaching of חכמים (from פרקי אבות) as her proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not talk too much with a woman

steps.confusionAlert: ברוריה does not say he should not have spoken to her. Her complaint is only that he used more words than he needed.

phrases.english: She said to him: Foolish Galilean,
didn't the Sages say this:
Do not talk much with a woman?!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא כָּךְ אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים: אַל תַּרְבֶּה שִׂיחָה עִם הָאִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the question in step 37 was worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: The length of רבי יוסי הגלילי's question
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: חכמים taught not to talk much with a woman, and he used extra words.

steps.title: ברוריה shows the shorter way to ask
steps.stepSummary: ברוריה tells him he should have asked using just two words: 'Which, to לוד?'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You should have said: Which to לוד?'
steps.whatsHappening: ברוריה finishes her rebuke by showing exactly how he should have asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She cuts his four words ('באיזו דרך נלך ללוד') down to two ('באיזה ללוד'). This proves he really did use extra words he did not need.
steps.whatToRemember: ברוריה won by showing that the same question could be asked in half the words, which fulfills the teaching of חכמים.

phrases.english: You should have said: 'Which to Lod?'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes ברוריה's rebuke by giving the correct wording.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The proper question needed only two words: 'באיזה ללוד.'

steps.title: ברוריה finds a student learning in a whisper
steps.stepSummary: A new story about ברוריה begins. She comes across a student who is reviewing his learning quietly, in a whisper.
steps.simpleTranslation: ברוריה came upon a certain student who was reviewing his learning in a whisper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about ברוריה. This line only sets the scene and gets ready for her reaction, which comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last story showed ברוריה's sharp mind, when she corrected רבי יוסי הגלילי for using too many words. Now the גמרא brings a second story about her. The key detail is that the student learned בלחישה, quietly and without saying the words out loud. This detail is what ברוריה will criticize next.

keyTerms.meaning: She found him / came across him
Reviewing or learning (going over the words of Torah)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that learning quietly is a good, humble thing here. The story is setting up a criticism. ברוריה will say that Torah should be said out loud, with the whole body involved.

phrases.english: Berurya came across a certain student
phrases.notes: Opens a second story about ברוריה.

phrases.english: who was reviewing his learning in a whisper.
phrases.notes: The detail that leads to her rebuke on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story of ברוריה and רבי יוסי הגלילי, the גמרא brings another story showing ברוריה's wisdom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scene-setting: a student was learning Torah in a whisper instead of out loud.
